newsitem.title: USA: Wet weather slows western US Midwest corn seedings.
newsitem.headline: Wet weather slows western US Midwest corn seedings.

text.p: Recent wet weather has caused a slow start in corn plantings in Iowa and Nebraska, and forecasts showing more rain could mean further delays, crop observers said Tuesday.

"In the southern three tiers of (Iowa) counties, less than 10 percent of the crop has been planted," said Mark Carlson, crop specialist for Iowa State University. "Pretty much the entire state has a 100 percent chance of rain today."
The U.S. Agriculture Department said Monday four percent of Iowa's corn crop had been planted as of Sunday, behind 20 percent a year ago and the 15-percent five-year average.
Carlson estimated that in central and north central Iowa, up to 40 percent of the corn crop had been seeded.
But fields in far southern Iowa remain saturated following heavy spring snows and rain, so some farmers have just begun to plant, Carlson said.
"In southern Iowa, we had 24 inches of snow not too long ago," Carlson said. "It's extrmely wet, and we're still trying to dry out the southern three tiers."
According to USDA's Iowa crop survey, topsoil moisture was rated 21 percent surplus and 76 percent adequate and subsoil moisture was rated 15 percent surplus and 81 percent adequate.
Although some planting progress has been made since the crop surveys were taken, U.S. meteorolgists show more rain is headed for the Corn Belt.

Beginning late Tuesday, two rain systems are expected to deliver up to inch of rain in Iowa and up to two inches of rain in eastern Nebraska, according to Joel Burgio, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. in Lexington, Mass.
USDA said that only six percent of Nebraska's corn crop was planted, also behind last year's pace of 23 percent and the average pace of 13 percent.
But farmers in Nebraska had a relatively clear weekend to plant corn, and cash sources there said good progress had been made since the government crop survey was taken.
"Overall, we haven't gotten a lot done here, but on Saturday, Sunday and yesterday (Monday) they (farmers) were really going after the crop," said a Omaha grain merchandiser.
Crop observers and cash dealers alike, said the expected rains would cause plantings in both states to grind to a halt once again.
In Illinois, another one of the U.S.'s top producing corn states, farmers are faring much better.
The pace of corn planting in Illinois has exceeded both the year-ago and average progress, USDA's crop data indicated.
USDA estimated Illinois corn plantings at 37 percent, well ahead of 27 percent last year and the 15-percent five-year average.

Concerns surfaced earlier about cool soil temperatures in Illinois and Indiana but early-week forecasts for temperatures near 70 degrees Fahrenheit should be warm enough to encourage germination in already-planted fields, grain dealers said.
"Fifty degrees (soil temperature) will give us the green light," said one Illinois dealer. "Everything that was planted yesterday is going to love this heat."
But efforts to seed the corn crop in Illinois could also slow this week because rain is expected to move into that area as well.
Late Tuesday, a storm system is forecast to bring 0.5 to 2.0 inches of rain to northern Illinois, while southern Illinois could receive 0.25 to 1.00 inch of rain through Wednesday, Burgio said.
